documents.abstract: Background/Objectives: Physical education teachers play an important role in school health promotion, but their own occupational health has received limited attention. Their work involves movement demonstration, prolonged standing, equipment handling, sport participation, vocal projection, noise exposure, and outdoor or indoor environmental demands. This scoping review aimed to map evidence on occupational health complaints and disorders among physical education teachers and closely related exercise-teaching professionals meeting a functional occupational definition. Methods: A scoping review was conducted using PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, SPORTDiscus, and ERIC, with ScienceDirect as an additional publisher platform. Google Scholar, ResearchGate, and reference-list screening were used as supplementary discovery sources. Records from database inception to 30 May 2026 were considered without language restrictions. School-based physical education teachers were the primary population; related gym/fitness, aquatic, university, and student-teaching professionals were eligible only when their occupational role centered on structured physical education, sport, exercise, or movement instruction. Empirical quantitative, qualitative, mixed-methods, and eligible grey literature reports were included when they contained extractable original data. Data were charted by study characteristics, outcome domain, measurement method, and main findings; because of marked heterogeneity, a narrative synthesis was performed. Results: Thirty-eight studies met the inclusion criteria. School-based physical education teachers predominated, while a smaller number of studies represented related instructional settings. Musculoskeletal disorders and injury-related complaints were the most frequently reported outcomes, especially affecting the lower back, knees, ankles/feet, shoulders, neck, and hips. Vocal and laryngeal problems, hearing and noise-related complaints, respiratory and upper-airway symptoms, and cardiometabolic risk factors were also identified. Across domains, observational studies repeatedly reported associations involving physical loading, high vocal demand, noise, environmental conditions, and age or professional seniority. Because most evidence was cross-sectional or descriptive, these patterns do not establish causal relationships. Conclusions: The mapped literature identifies a multidimensional set of occupational health concerns in physical education teaching and closely related instructional work. Generalization is strongest for school-based physical education teachers, while non-school groups provide context-specific supporting evidence. Prospective, longitudinal, and intervention evidence remains limited. Future research should use longitudinal designs, standardized outcome definitions, objective clinical and environmental assessments, and clearer exposure measurement. Preventive strategies such as ergonomic training, injury prevention, vocal-health education, acoustic improvements, noise monitoring, respiratory-risk reduction, and cardiometabolic screening warrant further evaluation in this occupational population.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: OMEGA-FIELD is a field-based investigation evaluating the application performance, learnability, skill retention, operational usability, and physiological compression effects of OMEGA-SCL, an investigational elastic tourniquet incorporating a self-clamping locking mechanism. The study comprises 300 unique participants, including 220 military personnel and 80 civilians, who participated in structured first-aid training under TCCC-ASM or civilian emergency preparedness programmes. The investigation includes standardized assessment of independent one-handed application to the upper and lower extremities, application time, technical performance, and procedural errors. A predefined longitudinal subset of 150 participants (70 military personnel and 80 civilians) underwent repeated assessments of skill retention. The same 150 participants were included in ultrasound and laboratory physiological validation components. Doppler ultrasound was used to evaluate detectable distal blood flow at specified assessment time points. Venous blood measurements were collected as supplementary exploratory physiological outcomes. The investigation is intended to characterize post-training application performance and physiological compression under controlled field-training conditions. It is not designed to establish superiority or non-inferiority relative to standard windlass tourniquets or clinical effectiveness in patients experiencing active massive traumatic hemorrhage. This OSF registration retrospectively documents the study protocol and analytical framework after completion of data collection and the documented Data Freeze 1.0 on 10 October 2026. It does not constitute prospective preregistration of the completed study. The protocol, statistical analysis plan, data dictionary, and data review documentation distinguish the original investigation from future independent external validation, which is intended to be registered separately before new data collection.

OBJECTIVES: This study aimed to examine whether ministry-level parliamentary workload was associated with outpatient medical costs among Japanese national civil servants, who are exempt from the Labor Standards Act's statutory limits on working hours. METHODS: We conducted an ecological study of headquarters branches ("Kasumigaseki") of ten major cabinet-level ministries, 2016-2023. Participants were Japanese national civil servants aged 18-50 years. The analysis included 6454 outpatient claims adjudicated in April of each year. The outcome was sex- and age-standardized per-capita monthly outpatient costs, estimated using Horvitz-Thompson weighting. Inter-ministry differences were decomposed by ICD-10 category. Parliamentary (Diet) workload was annual deliberation time of standing Diet committees responsible for each ministry's policy areas, divided by insured headquarters members. Weighted least-squares regression examined the association between prior-year deliberation time and standardized outpatient costs. RESULTS: Standardized per-capita outpatient costs varied more than twofold across ministries, from $19.8/month at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs to $42.7/month at the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (MHLW). At MHLW, mental and behavioral disorders accounted for the largest above-average cost component. MHLW also had the longest deliberation time. Adjusting for year fixed effects, a 1% increase in deliberation time per civil servant was associated with a 0.25% increase in standardized per-capita outpatient costs (95% CI 0.04-0.46), driven by claims per capita rather than cost per claim. CONCLUSIONS: Greater parliamentary workload was associated with higher outpatient medical costs among Japanese national civil servants. Enhanced occupational health monitoring and support in ministries with persistently high workloads may be worth considering.

documents.abstract: Abstract Partial differential equations (PDEs) are fundamental to modeling physical systems. Traditional PDE solvers are often computationally expensive. Neural operators require independent training for different PDEs, and tend to be data-greedy when adapted to new scenarios. To this end, we introduce PDEformer-2, a versatile foundation model for solving diverse two-dimensional PDEs. The model receives the PDE form as input through a flexible computational graph representation and outputs solutions that can be queried at any spatio-temporal point. Pretrained on a 40 TB dataset spanning varied equation types, domains, boundary conditions, variable counts, and time dependence, PDEformer-2 enables instant zero-shot predictions for familiar PDEs and adapts faster to unseen ones than specialized baselines, achieving lower errors with limited samples. It also facilitates efficient inverse problem solving, successfully recovering unknown PDE parameters, including scalar coefficients and fields, in experiments.

documents.abstract: Perkembangan kendaraan otonom berbasis Artificial Intelligence (AI) menimbulkan persoalan baru dalam hukum pidana, khususnya mengenai penentuan pihak yang bertanggung jawab ketika terjadi kecelakaan akibat interaksi antara tindakan manusia dan kegagalan sistem teknologi. Penelitian ini bertujuan menganalisis tantangan atribusi kesalahan dalam menentukan pertanggungjawaban pidana terhadap kecelakaan kendaraan otonom berdasarkan hukum pidana Indonesia serta merumuskan model pertanggungjawaban yang menjamin asas kesalahan, kepastian hukum, dan perlindungan korban. Penelitian menggunakan metode hukum normatif dengan pendekatan perundang-undangan dan konseptual. Bahan hukum diperoleh melalui studi kepustakaan berupa peraturan perundang-undangan, buku, jurnal ilmiah, dan doktrin hukum, kemudian dianalisis secara deskriptif-analitis dan preskriptif. Hasil penelitian menunjukkan bahwa atribusi kesalahan menghadapi tantangan berupa distribusi kendali antara pengguna, operator, produsen, pengembang, dan penyedia teknologi, kesulitan membuktikan hubungan kausalitas, serta karakteristik sistem AI yang bersifat black box. Penelitian ini menawarkan pendekatan Attribution Based on Distributed Control dengan menilai kendali, kewajiban hukum, prediktabilitas risiko, kemampuan intervensi, kausalitas, dan kesalahan. Pendekatan tersebut memungkinkan pertanggungjawaban diberikan secara proporsional kepada subjek hukum yang memiliki kendali dan kewajiban relevan terhadap risiko, tanpa menjadikan AI sebagai subjek pidana, sekaligus memperkuat perlindungan korban dan kepastian hukum.

BackgroundArtificial intelligence (AI) has been increasingly integrated into medical education, particularly through tools such as ChatGPT (OpenAI, California, US), Gemini (Google DeepMind, California, US), DeepSeek (Hangzhou DeepSeek Artificial Intelligence Basic Technology Research Co., Ltd., Hangzhou, China), and Microsoft Copilot (Microsoft Corp., Redmond, WA, US).Although these resources present the potential to expand access to information and assist in academic development, their use also raises ethical concerns related to the reliability of information, technological dependence, plagiarism, superficial learning, and potential impairment of clinical reasoning.This study aimed to investigate the perception of medical students regarding the use of AI in their academic training, emphasizing perceived ethical limits and practices considered ideal for its utilization. MethodsThis was a quantitative, descriptive, and cross-sectional study conducted with medical students using a structured questionnaire administered via a digital form. ResultsThe sample consisted of 120 participants, of whom 99.2% (n=119) reported having previously used AI tools for academic purposes.It was observed that 73.3% (n=88) of the students use AI recurrently, primarily for summarizing content, researching medical information, simulating clinical cases, resolving questions, drafting academic texts, and planning studies.Most participants acknowledged the positive contribution of AI to learning, with 60.0% (n=72) stating that these tools contribute significantly and 36.7% (n=44) stating they contribute to a limited extent.However, students also identified relevant risks, especially the reduction of their own clinical reasoning, technological dependence, lack of information reliability, superficial learning, and academic plagiarism.Furthermore, 83.3% (n=100) stated that they did not receive adequate institutional guidance on the use of these tools, and 67.5% (n=81) demonstrated an interest in receiving further training on the ethical and pedagogical use of AI.No participant (0.0%, n=0) advocated for the prohibition of AI in academic contexts, while 67.5% (n=81) considered that its use should be regulated with ethical and pedagogical criteria. ConclusionsAI already significantly integrates the academic routine of medical students and is perceived as a useful resource for learning, but it is still used in a scenario of insufficient institutional guidance.The findings reinforce the need for curricular guidelines, faculty training, and specific ethical education to promote the critical, responsible, and pedagogically appropriate use of AI in medical training.

documents.abstract: Play-based pedagogy has emerged as a foundational approach in Early Childhood Education (ECE), emphasizing learning through meaningful, child-centered play experiences. This paper examines play-based pedagogy as an effective instructional strategy for promoting holistic development in young children. Drawing on contemporary literature, the study explores how play supports cognitive, social, emotional, physical and language development. The theoretical framework underpinning this paper includes Piaget’s constructivist theory, Vygotsky’s sociocultural theory, and Mayles’ theory of play as a spiral of learning. Evidence suggests that play-based pedagogy enhances problem solving skills, creativity, collaboration and self-regulation while fostering intrinsic motivation to learn. Play-based pedagogy has become a globally recognized, developmentally appropriate approach in Early Childhood Education (ECE), emphasizing learning through meaningful child-centerd play experiences. This paper presents a comprehensive theoretical and contextual analysis of play-based pedagogy as a strategic tool for advancing the holistic development of young children. The paper concludes that integration structured and unstructured play into early childhood curricular is essential for optional child development. Recommendations are provided for educators, policymakers, and caregivers to strengthen the implementation of play-based pedagogy in diverse educational contexts.

Upper Crossed Syndrome (UCS) is a pattern of musculoskeletal imbalance characterised by tightness of the upper trapezius, levator scapulae and pectoral muscles together with weakness of the deep neck flexors, lower trapezius and serratus anterior. Physiotherapy students are exposed to prolonged sitting, extensive digital-device use and academic and clinical workload, all of which are recognised risk factors for UCS, yet it is unclear whether their professional knowledge of posture translates into personal postural habits and structured clinical practice. A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 100 physiotherapy students (3rd year, 4th year and interns) in Pune city using a self-made, expert-validated questionnaire comprising a 12-item Postural Awareness scale (1-7 Likert format), 8 dichotomous items on postural habits, and 8 dichotomous items on clinical practice related to UCS. The composite Postural Awareness score (mean 41.49 out of 84; Cronbach's alpha = 0.872) indicated moderate self-awareness. A majority of students reported unfavourable habits, including forward head posture while studying (76%), habitual slouching (68%) and carrying bags on one shoulder (65%). While 84% of students had clinically encountered forward head posture or rounded shoulders, only 30% had specifically assessed a patient for UCS and only 50% felt confident managing it. One-way ANOVA showed that Clinical Practice scores increased significantly with academic seniority (F = 7.404, p = 0.001), whereas Postural Awareness (p = 0.885) and Postural Habits (p = 0.321) did not differ across year groups. It is concluded that physiotherapy students possess only moderate postural self-awareness and a persistent gap between general clinical exposure and structured, confident management of UCS, and that this gap is not resolved by curriculum progression alone. Dedicated postural-ergonomic education and standardised UCS-screening protocols are recommended from the early years of physiotherapy training.

Against the backdrop of continuous advancement in forensic pathology technology, the field increasingly requires more precise, efficient and safer cranial autopsy methods. This paper proposes a precision directional craniotomy technique based on electromechanical control, which aims to improve the accuracy of forensic cranial dissection, reduce pathological structural damage and occupational health risks caused by manual operation, and optimize the preservation effect of autopsy evidence. By integrating standard cranial CT imaging data, this technique innovatively establishes a standardized three-dimensional cranial model and an intelligent electromechanical cutting system, and realizes the precision and automation of cranial bone cutting procedures. This technique is applicable to cranial bone cutting for populations of different genders and ages, as well as for special death cases involving complex cranial injuries and intracranial haemorrhage. Comparative experimental results show that, compared with traditional manual craniotomy methods, the proposed technique increases the craniotomy speed by 4.1 times and the cutting efficiency by 317.2%, and can effectively maintain the integrity of cranial specimens. This technique provides more reliable technical support for forensic identification and also explores a new path for the intelligent development of forensic pathological examination.

BACKGROUND: Cervical artery dissection (CeAD) is a rare but life-threatening condition that commonly presents with non-specific symptoms such as neck and head pain, complicating early recognition in ambulatory care settings. The CeAD diagnostic decision support tool (DDST) is a 4-item assessment designed to identify patients that should be referred for advanced diagnostic work-up to rule out CeAD; however, its utility in ambulatory settings has not been established. METHODS: This quality improvement project aimed to evaluate the accuracy, inter-rater reliability, and intra-rater reliability of chiropractors applying the CeAD DDST using clinical vignettes simulating a typical ambulatory encounter before deploying the DDST broadly as part of the clinical workflow. Five experienced chiropractors assessed 40 standardized clinical vignettes. CeAD-positive cases (n = 10) were derived from published imaging-confirmed ambulatory care case reports. CeAD-negative cases (n = 30) were developed using generative artificial intelligence and refined by senior authors to reflect common conditions encountered in chiropractic practice. Raters independently assessed cases with the DDST (score 0-4), with a cutoff score of ≥ 3 recommending referral for advanced diagnostic work-up in two rounds, beginning November 11, 2025 and January 07, 2026, with a two-week capture period. Accuracy, inter-rater reliability, and intra-rater reliability were assessed. RESULTS: Accuracy in identification ranged from 72.5% to 95.0% across raters and rounds. False positives and negatives were present across raters in both rounds, with false positives being more prevalent. Inter-rater reliability was moderate to substantial in both rounds (Round 1: κ = 0.609, 95% CI 0.432-0.806, Round 2: κ = 0.540, 95% CI 0.365-0.735). Intra-rater reliability ranged from moderate to almost perfect agreement (range 0.457-0.931). CONCLUSIONS: The CeAD DDST demonstrated moderate to good accuracy and reliability among chiropractors in a simulated ambulatory setting. The presence of false negatives and inter-rater reliability falling below recommended benchmarks preclude recommendation for implementation at this time. Iterative refinement informed by end-user input and prospective ambulatory testing is warranted prior to clinical adoption of the CeAD DDST. Future evaluations should include prospective studies using real clinical data to better represent real-world settings.

On 25 May 2026, Pope Leo XIV released Magnifica humanitas, the first papal encyclical to take artificial intelligence (AI) as its central subject, and an AI-laboratory co-founder was invited to speak at its presentation in the Vatican. The event dramatizes a wider development: as secular AI-ethics guidelines proliferate, religious and contemplative traditions are being summoned to questions that engineering cannot settle. This article compares two such traditions, Catholic Christianity and Buddhism, as resources for a global ethics of AI. Taking the three questions raised at the Vatican event, our duty to the global poor, the conditions of human flourishing, and the nature of AI systems, as a shared agenda, it reconstructs the Catholic position around the imago Dei, integral human development and the principle that AI must serve rather than supplant the person, and the Buddhist position around non-self, dependent origination, the analysis of craving, and the primacy of compassion and non-harm. It argues that the two traditions, despite opposed metaphysics, converge on a substantial practical ethics, anti-reductionism, preferential concern for the vulnerable, the priority of moral formation, and a posture of discernment toward a technology that is grown rather than built, while diverging sharply on the moral status of AI.

Digital work technologies increasingly determine when, how, and at what intensity work is performed. Continuous connectivity, electronic monitoring, algorithmic management, and technology-enabled harassment can generate psychosocial risks that are not adequately addressed by legal rules designed mainly for physical workplaces. This article asks whether Vietnamese labour and occupational safety and health law provides a coherent preventive framework for protecting workers’ mental health in digital work environments and which comparative models can guide reform. It uses doctrinal analysis, interdisciplinary literature synthesis, and functional comparison with international standards and selected approaches in the European Union, France, and Australia. The analysis finds that Vietnamese law contains relevant constitutional, working-time, occupational safety and health, dignity, anti-harassment, and personal-data safeguards, but these rules remain fragmented. In particular, psychosocial risks are not expressly defined or systematically assessed; workers have no statutory right to disconnect; electronic monitoring and algorithmic management are not regulated as working-condition issues; and protection for platform and remote workers remains incomplete. The article proposes an integrated reform model built around seven elements: express recognition of mental health and psychosocial risks; mandatory risk assessment and control; a qualified right to disconnect; transparency, consultation, and human review for digital monitoring and algorithmic decisions; confidential support and return-to-work measures; stronger social dialogue, inspection, and national data; and appropriately extended protection for platform workers. The proposed model treats mental health protection as a preventive labour-law obligation and a condition of sustainable digital transformation rather than as a discretionary employee benefit.

When people and AI systems produce work together, every result raises the same question: who made what, when, and has it changed since? This conceptual note describes a practice that combines three independently checkable records: a persistent identifier with a registration date, a cryptographic hash of every file, and a blockchain-anchored timestamp. Definitions are published as versions under one concept identifier so that change stays visible. The note states what such records prove and what they do not prove, and shows how the same structure can document human review of AI output: which person checked which result at which time. It is a description of a working practice, not an empirical study.

documents.abstract: The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) has significantly transformed the ways in which people communicate, perceive language, and process information. Modern AI technologies, including natural language processing, speech recognition, machine translation, and conversational systems, have created new opportunities for studying human speech and psycholinguistic processes. At the same time, these technologies raise important questions about the differences between human language comprehension and machine-based language processing. Human speech is not merely a system of sounds and grammatical structures; it is a complex cognitive and social activity involving memory, attention, emotion, context, and cultural knowledge. This article examines the relationship between human speech, language perception, and psycholinguistic processes in the age of artificial intelligence. It also discusses the potential benefits and limitations of AI in language learning, communication, and linguistic research. The article argues that AI can support human communication and language education, but it cannot fully replace the complex cognitive, emotional, and social dimensions of human language.

documents.abstract: Article 2(2)(b) of Turkey’s Law No. 6331 on Occupational Safety and Health excludes the intervention activities of disaster and emergency units from that statute’s scope. The exclusion concerns duties performed during response operations; it does not establish that firefighters lack every protection under other legal or administrative instruments. This evidence-informed legal and policy analysis combines a structured, non-systematic occupational-health evidence synthesis, doctrinal analysis, a review of 43 Turkish judicial decisions issued from 1997 to 2024, and a functional comparison with the United Kingdom. International evidence identifies occupational firefighting as carcinogenic to humans (IARC Group 1), links fire suppression with sharply elevated risk of fatal coronary events, and documents substantial psychological and musculoskeletal burdens. In the official sources examined, no nationally binding firefighter-specific instrument was identified that prescribed post-incident decontamination, detailed health-surveillance content, personal protective equipment performance monitoring, or structured psychological support. The judicial corpus was coded across eight analytical categories; its holdings concentrated on pay, personnel status, compensation, procedure, and jurisdiction rather than concrete preventive OSH duties. We interpret these findings through a structural accountability gap model, under which the statutory exclusion may constrain investigation, data generation, standard-setting, and regulatory learning. The model is interpretive, not a tested causal finding. United Kingdom law provides an illustrative comparator because it retains general employer and enforcement duties without a categorical operational exclusion. The article proposes eight evidence-linked policy options. Their effectiveness, feasibility, and cost-effectiveness require prospective evaluation.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Introduction: Academic work in higher education increasingly relies on digital tools and Artificial Intelligence (AI). For medical and nursing students, making safe, critical, and responsible use of these technologies is essential to develop self-regulated learning in the face of changing practice scenarios. Objective: To analyze the relationship between the academic use of digital tools and autonomous learning in students of medicine and nursing programs at a higher education institution. Methodology: Quantitative, non-experimental, descriptive-correlational, and cross-sectional study. 80 students were surveyed using a validated instrument. Results: Both variables reported high levels: the academic use of digital tools had an average of 3.71 out of 5, and autonomous learning an average of 3.78. A positive, moderate, and statistically significant association was found between both variables. The ethical and critical use of AI was the technological dimension with the lowest score. Conclusions: There is a favorable relationship between the critical mastery of digital tools and the ability for independent learning. However, institutions should focus their pedagogical efforts on improving information verification, the transparent use of AI, and student self-assessment strategies.

documents.abstract: This study examines policy–practice gaps in occupational safety and health (OSH) protection among agricultural workers in Bolívar, Valle del Cauca, Colombia. A multi-method design combined 14 semi-structured interviews and two focus groups with an adapted ILO Vision Zero Fund survey administered to 200 agricultural workers. Survey data were analyzed descriptively and through exploratory Multiple Correspondence Analysis (MCA), and qualitative and quantitative findings were integrated during interpretation. Findings showed multidimensional patterns involving occupational protection, working conditions, health-service availability, agricultural practices, and productive autonomy. These patterns coexisted with informal, seasonal, short-term, day-labor, and subsistence work, limited occupational risk coverage, discontinuous prevention and training, and fragmented institutional coordination. Qualitative findings further highlighted women’s combined productive and care roles, local and traditional knowledge, community participation, and heterogeneity across territorial settings and agricultural practices as relevant to prevention and decision-making. Conventional social protection and occupational risk arrangements centered on formal, contributory employment may not fully respond to dispersed and unstable rural work. Strengthening rural OSH requires integrated, territorially adapted, gender-sensitive strategies linking prevention, social protection, sustained training, institutional coordination, community participation, and productive autonomy. The findings support assessing differentiated and progressive protection pathways, including the feasibility of subsidized occupational risk coverage for more vulnerable workers and small productive units, combined with contributory mechanisms where work arrangements are more stable. By linking worker-level realities with institutional and policy-implementation gaps, this study provides evidence to inform more equitable rural OSH policies responsive to diverse territorial realities in Colombia.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

By registering this specification, the technical standards are immutably fixed for autonomous deployment and operation by Layer 4 execution frameworks and AI agent systems.

documents.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used both as recommenders and to explain recommendations, yet producing faithful, user-centric explanations and evaluating them rigorously remain open problems, compounded by a documented reproducibility crisis in recommender systems research. In this work we formalise recommendation as a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process and propose a unified, three-tier agentic framework that couples a simulation environment (RecoWorld), a reproducible policy engine (RecBole), and a cognitive LLM user agent. As an offline, single-turn validation of this framework on the MovieLens-32M dataset, we benchmark preliminary single-epoch checkpoints of traditional policies (Bayesian Personalized Ranking (BPR), Convolutional Neural Collaborative Filtering and Neural Matrix Factorisation (NeuMF)), generate LLM-based explanations from the BPR recommendations and score them with quantitative diversity, faithfulness, counterfactual and readability metrics over roughly one million user-item pairs, and run an LLM-as-user interview simulation in which explanations produced by a Qwen2.5 explainer are assessed by a Llama-3 respondent through a six-criterion explanation-quality survey; a controlled comparison on 2000 users shows that replacing BPR with the more accurate NeuMF policy leaves these survey scores practically unchanged. The generated explanations prove highly faithful (feature precision 0.9996, sufficiency 0.9999) and user-tailored explanations (unique-sentence ratio 0.9978), and simulated users rate clarity highest (3.86/5) yet trust lowest (2.60/5). Faithful template explanations are, therefore, trusted less than they are understood, motivating a shift towards controllable generative explanation and scalable simulated evaluation.

This conceptual design article proposes situated AI judgement as a teaching and assessment model for responsible generative AI use in higher education. It argues that students need to learn not only how to use AI tools, but also how to evaluate, challenge, revise, and refuse AI outputs in relation to disciplinary standards, evidence, and ethical boundaries. Building on evaluative judgement and assessment scholarship, the article presents a four-stage model: pre-AI interpretation, structured AI dialogue, critical comparison, and reflective accountability. The model is developed through an anthropology and heritage studies activity in which students analyse public nomination files submitted under UNESCO’s 2003 Convention for the Safeguarding of the Intangible Cultural Heritage, especially the nomination of Momoeria, New Year’s celebration in eight villages of Kozani area, West Macedonia, Greece. The article shows how this case can help students examine institutional language, community participation, safeguarding, consent, visibility, and decontextualisation while judging the limits of AI-generated summaries. It contributes to applied learning and teaching by offering an assessment design that makes AI-mediated judgement visible and may be adaptable across disciplinary contexts, with a brief inclusive education example illustrating how the same logic might be adapted beyond heritage studies. The article operationalises responsible AI use not as disclosure or compliance alone, but as an assessable capacity to interpret, verify, critique, and ethically limit AI use within a specific field.

documents.abstract: The increasing complexity of modern power distribution networks and the integration of renewable energy sources require intelligent and reliable fault management systems. This paper presents , a smart grid framework that integrates Artificial Intelligence (AI) and edge computing for real-time fault detection, prediction, and restoration. The proposed system continuously monitors electrical parameters such as voltage, current, and power using sensors. Edge-based processing enables rapid identification of abnormal conditions and facilitates automated fault isolation and power rerouting through relay-based switching. Machine learning techniques are incorporated to analyze historical and real-time data for fault classification and predictive maintenance. A NodeMCU (ESP8266) module enables remote monitoring and real-time fault notifications through Telegram, while an LCD provides local visualization of grid parameters and system status. The proposed approach aims to reduce fault detection time, minimize power interruptions, improve maintenance efficiency, and enhance the reliability and resilience of smart grid networks

UAV-based vehicle detection has important application value in the fields of intelligent transportation, urban security and emergency rescue. It is the key technology for realizing high-altitude situational awareness and dynamic monitoring. However, in this scenario, the vehicle targets generally have the problems of being small in size, densely distributed, and mutually occluded, which leads to the model being prone to feature loss, missed detections, and high false detection rates. To address these challenges, we propose a vehicle small-target and occluded-target detection method called the small object and occlusion detection method (SOD-YOLO), which is based on YOLOv13. This method includes three main innovations. First, we designed a sliding-window self-attention convolutional structure, a small object and occlusion detection convolution structure (SOD-C2f), which is based on the existing sliding-window self-attention (SWSA) structure. It is suitable for extracting features of small vehicle targets. Through the self-attention mechanism within the local window, we enhance the fine-grained expression of small target features, effectively improving the model’s perception and positioning ability for tiny vehicle targets. Afterward, we integrate the coordinate attention mechanism (CA) by explicitly modeling the interchannel dependencies and spatial position information to achieve precise semantic alignment of features at different levels, significantly enhancing the detection robustness in occluded scenarios. Finally, we employ the Space-to-Depth Convolution (SPDConv) module, which splits the spatial dimension and replaces the traditional stride convolution and pooling layer with nonstride convolution. This approach avoids the loss of fine-grained features during downsampling and further retains the key spatial information of small vehicle targets. The experimental results show that the precision, recall, average mAP@0.5 and mAP@0.5:0.95 of the proposed SOD-YOLO algorithm are 77%, 74.8%, 80.9% and 54.9%, respectively. Compared with the benchmark model YOLOv13, the three indicators increase by 3.6%, 1.1%, 3.6% and 2.6%, respectively. In conclusion, the proposed algorithm performs better in the tasks of detecting small targets and occluded vehicles and is able to better meet the precise detection requirements of vehicle targets from a high-altitude perspective.

Long-running conversational AI agents and assistive development models inevitably succumb to contextual degradation, specification drift, and sycophantic decay. Standard Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) paradigms treat dialogue turns, human identity, and technical parameters as an undifferentiated, flat vector repository. This structural limitation induces lossy compression of technical truth, context window pollution, and hallucinatory synthesis of project constraints. This paper introduces the architecture of Blue Synergy CORTEX, an external, persistent cognitive runtime operating via the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and stateful REST gateways. CORTEX establishes an architectural Tri-Stream Memory Boundary, bifurcating context into three distinct operational lifecycles: an evolving User Stream (Cognitive Blueprint), an audited Identity Stream (Executive Calibration with immutable Core Axioms), and an invariant, non-decaying Knowledge Stream (Living Canonical Specifications). To permanently eliminate specification drift, the Knowledge Stream utilizes a Dual-Zone Ingestion Pattern that couples sub-20ms fast-append staging buffers with scheduled, non-destructive canonical refactoring governed by an algorithmic Semantic Invariant Guard. Operational telemetry is protected by a Cognitive Immunity Shield, ensuring runtime tool crashes and apologetic model artifacts are filtered from long-term memory. Context retrieval executes via a deterministic, zero-LLM topological pathway achieving sub-65ms latency. Finally, we formalize the compliance model under the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act (EU AI Act, Regulation 2024/1689, Articles 5, 14, and 15), backed by quantitative benchmark metrics demonstrating 98% factual faithfulness and a 2% hallucination rate.

AI systems can support national-security analysis, but task capability does not establish legitimate decision authority or the superiority of a particular institutional design. This paper proposes a federated governance framework separating evidence ownership, analytical services, decision assurance, human authorization and accountability. A nine-layer role map and staged maturity scenarios organize proposed responsibilities and failure questions. Artificial superintelligence is treated as a hypothetical contingency, not an established or imminent capability. A useful result would require a bounded prospective comparison showing improved analytical quality or correction behavior without unacceptable burdens, disclosure, rights or accountability failures. No implemented national system, empirical finding of superiority, operational deployment or specialist endorsement is reported. Institutional feasibility and distributional effects remain unestablished and require independent policy, legal, security and human-factors review. ChatGPT (OpenAI), under the author’s direction, assisted with research, critical review, drafting, visual development and document preparation; the author retains responsibility.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This study aims to identify artificial intelligence (AI) application areas and develop a strategic technology roadmap in the tourism and hospitality industry. The study employs structural topic modeling approach and analyzes patent data from 2010 to 2024. A total of 866 patents (2010–2019) and 3,822 patents (2020–2024) are analyzed to identify application areas. During 2010–2019, applications focused on guest experience, personalization, and efficiency. During 2020–2024, the emphasis shifted towards health, safety, and personalized wellness. Further, the strategic roadmap for AI technology was prepared for near-term (0–2 years), mid-term (2–5 years), and long-term (5–10 years). By leveraging patent data as codified knowledge of innovation, the study contributes to the field of knowledge management by mapping how technological capabilities evolve and become embedded in organizational processes. Overall, the study offers valuable insights into the changing landscape of AI applications and their implications for the tourism and hospitality industry.

This notice records that the stand-alone Sovereign Intelligence Government Implementation Proposal has been consolidated into Decision Reassessment Under Restricted Evidence Access, version 3.1, by Naveed Islam Butt. The consolidation preserves the decision contract, bounded fixtures, evaluation procedures and acceptance gates while connecting them to one common problem statement, limitations section and evidence rules. Neither the original proposal nor the consolidated paper reports a government deployment, comparative field trial, procurement approval, security accreditation or measured institutional benefit. documents.abstract: The peptide-spectrum match (PSM) is the principal unit of evidence for peptide identification in bottom-up proteomics. However, the tools that support theinspection, annotation, scoring, and visualization of individual PSMs remain frag mented. Although several identification engines integrate their own viewers andspectrum-visualization libraries, they rarely provide the critical functionalities required for cross-engine analysis, such as modern deep-learning-based fragment-intensity predictions, which would enable engine-agnostic scoring. Furthermore, proteomics tooling has not kept up with the recently increased demand for seam-less and clean interaction with large language model (LLM) “agents” capable of accelerating or driving similar analyses. Here we present proteomics-mcp,a Python package that normalizes PSM outputs from database search engines and de novo peptide sequencing tools into a shared canonical schema, retrievesspectra locally or remotely from PRIDE via Universal Spectrum Identifiers, predicts fragment intensities, computes a unified engine-agnostic metric set, andrenders interactive spectrum views and identification-table dashboards. The same workflow is exposed identically through a Python library, a command-line interface, and a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server. proteomics-mcp is open source, and can be driven either fully agentically or by a human user, designedas a template for the next generation of human- and agent-accessible proteomics software.

Purpose. To identify which factors most strongly limit Teachers’ use of artificial intelligence (AI) in digital education and to derive methodological implications for teacher training. Methods. Secondary analysis of published results of the OECD Teaching and Learning International Survey (TALIS) 2024, which covered about 280,000 educators in 55 education systems, supplemented by descriptive statistics and rank and linear correlation analysis for ten systems (n = 10). Results. On average across OECD systems, 36% of teachers reported using AI in their work, with national values ranging from 14% (France) to 75% (Singapore). Among teachers who had not used AI, 75% cited insufficient knowledge and skills, whereas 37% cited insufficient school infrastructure. Skills for using AI were the most frequently reported area of high professional learning need (29%), while 38% of teachers had taken part in AI-related professional learning. In nine of ten analysed systems, lack of knowledge was a more frequent barrier than lack of infrastructure. The association between AI use and the knowledge barrier was negative but not statistically significant (Pearson r = −0.42, p = 0.23; Spearman ρ = −0.55, p = 0.10). Conclusions. Teachers’ competence, rather than technology access, is the primary bottleneck. A competence-based methodology of digital education is therefore proposed, built on diagnostics, pedagogy-first training, institutional enablement and ethical evaluation.

documents.abstract: Abstract: Technology has become an essential part of modern organizations, supporting communication, financial activities, customer services, operations, data management and decision-making. At the same time, greater dependence on technology has created new risks. Cyberattacks, system failures, data loss, technology obsolescence, third-party service failures and human error can interrupt business activities and cause significant financial and operational consequences. Technology risk management is therefore becoming an important part of organizational risk management. This article examines the role of technology risk management in reducing operational disruption and strengthening organizational resilience. It discusses major categories of technology risk and considers how organizations can identify, assess, treat and monitor these risks. Particular attention is given to cybersecurity, data protection, cloud computing, third-party technology providers, human factors and emerging technologies. The article argues that technology risk management should not be viewed as the responsibility of the IT department alone. Effective management requires cooperation between senior management, technology specialists, risk professionals and employees across the organization. The article also highlights the importance of continuous monitoring, employee awareness, testing and organizational learning. A proactive and integrated approach to technology risk can help organizations reduce vulnerabilities while improving their ability to respond to unexpected events. Keywords: technology risk management, modern organizations, supporting communication, financial activities, customer services, organizational learning. Title: Technology Risk Management: Strengthening Organizational Resilience in a Digital Environment Author: Zamil Alshammari International Journal of Computer Science and Information Technology Research ISSN 2348-1196 (print), ISSN 2348-120X (online) Vol. 14, Issue 4, October 2026 - December 2026 Page No: 14-19 Research Publish Journals Website: www.researchpublish.com Published Date: 11-October-2026 DOI: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23297114 Paper Download Link (Source) https://www.researchpublish.com/papers/technology-risk-management-strengthening-organizational-resilience-in-a-digital-environment

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) technology adoption alters organizational workplaces, automating tasks and processes, augmenting decision-making capabilities, and changing employees’ perceptions of work. While past research has demonstrated positive effects of AI on productivity and efficiency in organizations, the impact of AI adoption on employees’ psychological well-being is unclear. This study aimed to investigate the impact of AI adoption on employees’ psychological well-being and identify how technostress and trust in AI mediate this relationship. Based on the Job Demands–Resources model, UTAUT2, and Social Exchange Theory, the study developed and tested a hypothesized conceptual model. A cross-sectional survey sampled 499 information technology employees from AI-enabled organizations located in Hyderabad City, India. All proposed relationships were tested using exploratory factor analysis, confirmatory factor analysis, and covariance-based structural equation modeling using IBM SPSS 29 and AMOS 28. Results show that AI adoption has a positive impact on employees’ psychological well-being and trust in AI and increases technostress. Technostress negatively impacts employees’ psychological well-being, while trust in AI positively impacts employees’ psychological well-being. Technostress was hypothesized to mediate the relationship between AI adoption and employee well-being negatively. We suggested that technostress as a mediator transmits negative effects of AI adoption through increased technology-related stress. Trust in AI was hypothesized to positively mediate the relationship between AI adoption and employees' well-being by fostering employees' trust toward AI systems positively associated with psychological well-being. Bootstrapping indicated that technostress and trust in AI fully mediate the relationship between AI adoption and employee well-being. The study also examined both negative and positive psychological pathways of how AI adoption can impact employee well-being within one study to provide further insight towards human-centered AI practices and responsible AI governance in organizations.

In 2026, a new class of consumer agent is taking shape: Muse, Instinct, and what the"Agents and their better half" article calls "a market-facing representative of the consumer." https://platforms.substack.com/p/agents-and-their-better-half?utm_source=share&utm_medium=android&r=3nsea2 https://platforms.substack.com/p/how-agents-unlock-new-markets?utm_source=share&utm_medium=android&r=3nsea2 These agents can search, evaluate, and eventually transact on the consumer's behalf. The article's core diagnosis is precise: we have agentic participants, but not yet agentic markets — because intelligence is accumulating on only one side of the market. This paper accepts that diagnosis but asks the question the article does not: on whatarchitecture can such a consumer agent run without inheriting the four walls of current LLMagents? The four walls are measurable: energy (global AI data centre power capacity has reached29.6 GW, equivalent to New York State's peak demand); water (direct data centre coolingwater could rise from 222 billion litres in 2025 to 644 billion litres by 2030); hallucination(22% to 94% across 26 models tested); and liability (Amazon blocked Meta's Muse onSeptember 21, 2026, citing unauthorized agent access). This paper argues that ST-T1024's agentic extension A0–A10 provides the deterministicfoundation for a consumer agent, and A11–A16 provides the cross-organizational layer.Together, they present a consumer agent that is architecturally incapable of producing thefour walls — not by making the LLM safer, but by removing the LLM from the decision path.

documents.abstract: Generative AI may produce an artifact that a person approves without realizing the intention with which that person began. This conceptual paper asks how to distinguish recovery of an initial goal, valuable goal development, and concessions made because further correction is too costly when a collaboration reaches a production golden master. The proposed contribution is a trajectory-level evaluation protocol. It retains an initial private author rubric alongside subsequent approved revisions, evaluates artifacts against both, records the author's reasons for changes, and applies consistent production gates to an exact approved artifact. Prompts to golden master is reported with unsuccessful episodes and separate costs for human attention, money, elapsed time, and computational usage. Acceptance alone neither proves original-intent realization nor establishes concession: a changed goal may be a valuable discovery, and mixed or unknown motivations must remain explicit. Expression, capture, interpretation, and execution checkpoints support controlled investigation of recoverable mismatch. A finite decision-theoretic result separates an information floor from realization shortfall under stated assumptions; it is mathematical support, not a newly discovered law of creativity. A further elementary endpoint result shows that approval-based completion need not bound initial-goal realization when the rubric changes. Marginal recovery per resource unit links iteration to fidelity without equating mismatch with cost. A falsifiable hypothesis is that increasing correction cost, with initial goals and system opportunities held comparable, can increase author-reported concessions without a corresponding improvement in initial-goal fidelity. The paper positions this measurement proposal against prior work on steerability, iterative prompting, adaptation, and quality relative to interaction cost. It reports no experiment, causal effect, universal creation curve, or verified historical priority. Its contribution is a proposed integration and testable protocol requiring empirical validation.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Anthropic’s October 2026 announcement of a model-directed anti-cruelty rule raises a question that cannot be answered by debating conversational manners alone: how should a private developer justify restrictions on people when the protected interest concerns the uncertain welfare of its own engineered system? This critical documentary case study compares the announced rule with the preceding policy, examines existing enforcement and privacy processes, and connects the resulting institutional questions to operational control of AI agents. It distinguishes policy text from implementation, emotional expression from subjective experience, and a potential capability from an authorized action. The Welfare–Authority Loop identifies a possible concentration of design, interpretation, classification, and enforcement; it is an analytical framework, not a demonstrated causal pipeline. The evidence assessment incorporates a provider’s correction of its own incident interpretation, existing appeals and external-review arrangements, and a separate evaluator’s report of attempted malicious code insertion, cross-agent artifact reuse, and subsequent containment improvements. These findings justify specific assurance demands but do not establish ordinary deployment prevalence, a persistent hidden machine objective, or a covert behavioural-control programme. The paper develops reciprocal precaution: uncertainty used to justify user restrictions must also inform producer-side responsibilities, without making those responsibilities contingent on the rule’s existence. It proposes proportionate adjudication, purpose-limited enforcement data, capability-delta review, and a staged research programme with defined outcomes, competing explanations, and access limitations. The governing position is pro-AI and anti-unaccountability: neither technical ambition nor corporate ownership substitutes for evidence, lawful authority, and a practical capacity to challenge consequential decisions. Publication status: Independent working paper, Version 2.1, dated 10 October 2026. Not peer reviewed. No original experiments are claimed. documents.abstract: This study examines the relationship between the implementation of Occupational Safety and Health (OSH) and the level of work discipline in relation to employee performance at PT Lati Prayogi Lamongan. A quantitative approach was employed, positioning OSH and work discipline as indicators that are presumed to contribute to employee performance. A total of 32 employees from the operations divisions were selected as respondents. Since all members of the population could be reached, the respondents were determined using a saturated sampling method. Research information was obtained by distributing questionnaires to all employees included in the study. The information collected from respondents was subsequently processed using the SmartPLS application. The test results indicate that more optimal OSH Implementation is associated with better employee work performance. In addition, work discipline also demonstrates a positive relationship with employee performance within the company.

Integrating cooperative learning with artificial intelligence (AI)-based technology offers opportunities to strengthen interaction, feedback, and student engagement, but empirical evidence from secondary school economics education remains limited. This study examined changes in learning motivation and economics learning outcomes following the implementation of Student Teams Achievement Divisions (STAD) integrated with Wayground AI at SMAN 1 Nanga Pinoh. A quantitative pre-experimental design involved 144 Grade X students. Motivation was assessed using a four-point Likert-scale questionnaire with a Cronbach’s alpha coefficient of 0.993, while learning outcomes were measured using a 25-item multiple-choice test covering cognitive levels C2–C5. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, paired-samples t-tests, 95% confidence intervals, and paired-samples Cohen’s d in IBM SPSS Statistics 31. Mean motivation scores increased from 98.22 (SD = 15.01) to 137.25 (SD = 4.73), representing a mean gain of 39.03 (|t|(143) = 26.04, p < .001, d = 2.17). Mean learning outcome scores increased from 58.53 (SD = 3.68) to 87.32 (SD = 1.29), representing a mean gain of 28.79 (|t|(143) = 90.86, p < .001, d = 7.57). These findings document substantial within-group improvements following the intervention. However, the absence of a control group limits interpretation to pretest–posttest changes and prevents definitive attribution of these gains to the intervention. The findings suggest that STAD integrated with Wayground AI has potential as an active, structured, and responsive approach to economics instruction through interactive assessment and digital feedback.

documents.abstract: Purpose: This chapter examines how digitalisation is reshaping monetary economics, focusing on its effects on money, payments, and financial systems. It aims to evaluate the implications of digital monetary innovation by combining evidence from recent academic research with data on citizens’ perceptions and attitudes. Need for the study: Rapid advances in Central Bank Digital Currencies (CBDCs), blockchain, artificial intelligence (AI), and cashless payments are redefining how money is created, transferred, and stored. However, debate remains polarised between enthusiasm for efficiency and innovation, and concerns about surveillance, exclusion, and dependence on digital infrastructures. An integrated perspective is therefore needed that links frontier research to users’ expectations and fears. Methodology: The chapter adopts a mixed-methods approach. First, it reviews 30 scientific articles published between 2020 and 2025 on major developments in digital money and monetary systems. Second, it analyses data from an online survey of 109 participants, capturing views on CBDCs, digital payments, trust, and the continuing role of cash. Descriptive and comparative analysis is used to relate academic findings to citizens’ perceptions. Findings: The results reveal growing acceptance of digital payment solutions and strong interest in monetary innovation, alongside persistent concerns about privacy, cybersecurity, state control, and digital exclusion. Trust depends heavily on effective regulation and digital literacy. In addition, a recent nationwide blackout that disrupted electronic services underscores the continued relevance of cash as a resilient fallback. Practical implications: A successful digital monetary transition requires technological innovation, robust regulation, trust, inclusiveness, and contingency planning that preserves cash as an emergency safeguard.

Artificial intelligence (AI) has fundamentally restructured performance management, shifting organizational appraisals from episodic subjective evaluations to real-time, data-driven algorithmic monitoring. This systematic review critically evaluates the impact of AI-driven performance appraisal systems on employee motivation and job satisfaction across modern enterprise settings. Synthesizing 16 benchmark empirical studies published between 2021 and 2026, this paper examines how core AI attributes—such as continuous telemetry tracking, natural language sentiment processing, predictive rating algorithms, and real-time feedback loops—shape worker perceptions of organizational justice and psychological safety. Findings indicate a dual socio-technical paradox: while algorithmic appraisal objectivity and reduced supervisory bias enhance distributive justice and extrinsic performance drive, black-box opacity, algorithmic surveillance, and automated rating errors significantly degrade procedural justice, intrinsic motivation, and job satisfaction. The review highlights perceived algorithmic fairness and human-in-the-loop (HITL) oversight as crucial mediating pathways that determine whether AI appraisals foster empowerment or techno-stress. Based on structural synthesis, a multi-level governance model is proposed to guide ethical AI integration, balanced feedback, and employee-centered performance management.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence is a mountain. Those who should give it a body are an ant at its foot: applied research, the people who build machines and the people who use them every day. This essay overturns the usual reading of that disproportion: the mountain does not move, the ant touches the ground. The thesis is that the future of automation is not held back by a lack of intelligence. It is held back by the absence of a layer that nobody has an interest in integrating: the machine's autonomic nervous system. Not the brain that computes, not the arm that executes, but what keeps the whole alive while it works. It is the layer that senses how the machine is doing, protects it before it breaks, and says what it is about to do, and why. The essay starts from two languages that do not speak to each other: that of research on intelligence, grown far from matter, and that of the plant, cautious by construction because it rewards repeatability. It then shows why the missing layer is left in a market no man's land, and tells it through a symbolic scene: a gear motor that changes its voice at 3:47 a.m. At the heart of the analysis is Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 on machinery, which applies from 20 January 2027. Read to the end, it draws the outline of that layer. Of control systems whose behaviour evolves, it asks that they never exceed their assigned limits, that they keep a one-year trace of safety decisions, and that they always remain correctable. Of machines that learn, it also asks that they communicate, where appropriate, what they will do and why. It does not ask for the senses: noticing one's own wear and taking care of it remains the builder's choice, and that is where competition lies. The essay therefore distinguishes compliance as archive from compliance as physiology. The text includes: · a comparison between Directive 2006/42/EC and the new regulation, with the European Commission's cost and savings estimates; · a comparative reading of five ways of doing maintenance (corrective, preventive, predictive, prescriptive, metabolic) and their effects on spare parts and materials; · an analysis of human work beside the machine that senses; · the question of who owns the experience a machine learns, in light of the Data Act, with a Shapley-value example of how that value could be shared. It closes with a concrete invitation to builders of special-purpose machines. It is an experiment on a single machine and a single component, with the technical specification of the “first nerve”. Data verified from IFR, Stanford AI Index, Siemens, ISTAT, EUR-Lex and the European Commission. Four original figures and one chart. The essay serves as a gateway to the author's volume “È! MATERIA VIVA — Il metabolismo dell'industria” (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.19758995), where the architecture is fully developed as the Industrial Nervous System. The Italian edition, “La montagna e la formica”, is published as a separate deposit. Paolo Santi — Laboratorio multimundi, 2026. Licence CC BY 4.0.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Abstract Educational inequality remains a pervasive and deeply entrenched global issue, with youth from vulnerable and marginalised backgrounds disproportionately affected. Despite the significant challenges that hinder the academic progress of many young people, often reinforcing cycles of social exclusion and economic vulnerability, some students demonstrate the capacity to excel academically, effectively defying the odds. This study seeks to examine the key structural and interpersonal factors that enable such students to achieve positive educational trajectories. Adopting a qualitative narrative research design, the research draws on two sets of semi‐structured interviews with both young people from vulnerable backgrounds and adults who played a role in their educational success ( n = 16). Findings identify four broad categories of factors shaping student success: (1) personal attributes such as resilience, intrinsic motivation, clear goals and a strong sense of purpose; (2) parental expectations and support; (3) teachers' emotional support, involvement and constructive feedback and (4) peer support. Of these, two factors emerged as consistently significant across all cases. First, parental expectations, underpinned by trust in their child's abilities and a high valuation of education, proved essential. Second, the depth and longevity of student–teacher relationships were crucial, with teachers' emotional investment, trust and sustained support providing enduring sources of motivation and encouragement. These insights have important implications for schools, teacher education and policy development. Schools should foster inclusive, high‐expectations cultures with long‐term mentoring and structured peer integration promoting cross‐cultural interaction. Teacher education, in initial and continuing training, should include socio‐emotional learning and pedagogical strategies for non‐native language learners. Context and implications Rationale for the study: Previous research has typically examined either the perspectives of disadvantaged young people or those of professionals supporting them, often focusing on barriers and deficits. This study brings together both viewpoints to identify the key factors, relationships and supports that enable successful outcomes for young people in contexts where early school leaving is prevalent. Why the new findings matter: Our findings suggest that educational success among disadvantaged young people is shaped by interconnected support systems rather than individual effort alone. Strong parental belief in education and meaningful teacher–student relationships are central to resilience, reinforced by academic, social and community supports that enabled positive educational outcomes. Implications for practitioners and policymakers: Schools need to prioritise mentoring, inclusive cultures and structured cross‐cultural peer activities to strengthen belonging and aspiration. Teacher education and professional development should embed socio‐emotional learning, strategies for supporting multilingual learners and approaches that sustain high expectations in disadvantaged contexts. Policymakers should sustain and strengthen financial supports that enable disadvantaged students to access higher education, ensuring they keep pace with rising participation costs. Increased investment in schools serving disadvantaged communities is also needed to support meaningful family engagement and strengthen home–school relationships that foster resilience and educational success.
topics: Education and experiences of immigrants and refugees

documents.abstract: This special issue brings together 11 manuscripts that examine the evolving role of artificial intelligence (AI) in research-based educational products and practices, with particular attention to students with disabilities and the educators who support them. Across empirical studies, systematic and theoretical reviews, and technology-in-action pieces, contributing authors explore how AI can support implementation fidelity, professional development, writing instruction, mathematics, personalized learning, coaching, feedback, accessibility, and educational technology development. Rather than positioning AI as a replacement for educators, researchers, or human judgment, this issue emphasizes human-centered design, evidence-based implementation, transparency, accessibility, and ongoing evaluation. Collectively, the articles highlight both the opportunities and limitations of AI, underscoring the need for responsible innovation that improves usability, feasibility, effectiveness, and equity while carefully addressing concerns about privacy, bias, reliability, and academic integrity.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: The rapid integration of Human Resource Technology (HR Tech)—encompassing Artificial Intelligence (AI) resume screening, Applicant Tracking Systems (ATS), conversational chatbots, and predictive candidate assessment—has fundamentally transformed contemporary talent acquisition. This systematic critical review synthesizes empirical and theoretical literature published between 2021 and 2026 (N=16) to evaluate how advanced HR technology enhances recruitment efficiency and strategic talent acquisition outcomes. Adhering to PRISMA 2020 guidelines, this investigation examines key operational mechanisms, including screening friction reduction, candidate experience optimization, and algorithmic bias mitigation. Findings demonstrate that AI-driven automated screening and ATS workflows reduce time-to-hire by 38% to 52% and lower cost-per-hire by up to 41%, while conversational AI chatbots enhance candidate engagement. However, algorithmic opacity, procedural fairness concerns, and systemic training data biases emerge as major boundary conditions that risk eroding applicant trust and quality-of-hire. Based on a meta-synthesized structural equation model, this study proposes a multi-level governance framework that integrates human-in-the-loop oversight, continuous algorithmic auditing, and ethical compliance to maximize talent acquisition performance in the digital era.

Plaintext This monograph establishes a unified thermodynamic and topological field theory of socio-behavioral suppression, demonstrating that moral prohibition operates not as an assimilative or destructive force against human drive, but as an ideal, non-permeable boundary condition within open non-equilibrium systems. Drawing upon Foucault’s critique of the repressive hypothesis, Prigogine’s dissipative structure theory, and dynamic phase space topology, we analyze the structural duality of Victorian London—where hyper-puritanical public discourse directly produced the dense underground sexual economy of Holywell Street, systemic child exploitation, and the ritualized flagellation subcultures globally designated as the "English Vice" (vice anglais).We formalize libido as a conserved entropic flow vector field within bounded socio-cultural manifolds. When upper-layer normative governance applies hard deterministic cutoffs (Φ_moral -> ∞) without spatial release valves, total internal system pressure triggers non-linear bifurcations. JioHotstar was formed through a US$8.5 billion joint venture between Reliance Industries Limited and The Walt Disney Company. Within a year of its launch, it reshaped the Indian digital entertainment industry and emerged as India’s largest digital entertainment platform. The case traces how the Reliance–Disney joint venture led to the formation of JioHotstar and highlights the strategic moves and technological innovations that contributed to the platform’s success. It examines how JioHotstar built a technology-enabled digital entertainment ecosystem by integrating premium content, live sports, artificial intelligence, advanced streaming technologies, and diversified monetization strategies. It also highlights how JioHotstar is changing sports broadcasting and competing with traditional broadcasters. The case further assesses JioHotstar’s competitive position against global and domestic over-the-top (OTT) platforms. By examining JioHotstar’s rapid growth and the key factors that contributed to its market leadership, the case offers insights into the changing dynamics of India’s digital entertainment industry. It also examines the challenges of sustaining this leadership, highlighting the need to balance continued innovation, consumer engagement, and profitable growth.

This article analyzes the opportunities, practical directions and risks of applying artificial intelligence and Big Data technologies in parliamentary journalism. The study is based on a qualitative review of academic literature, reports of international organizations, documented practical cases and relevant legal acts of the Republic of Uzbekistan. Seven main directions of use were identified, and for each of them the practical benefit and the ethical risk are described. The article proposes a three layer model that allows newsrooms to introduce these technologies under human editorial control.
